title: Dead unformed faith still first disposition to justice (Stapleton)
source_text: XVII. Porro quamvis Scholae Romanae Theologi fateantur & agnoscant fidem mortuam & informem ad salutem non prodesse, & ad justitiam esse inutilem, quod inter alios expresse, idque multis in locis, asserit Thomas Stapletonus, docent tamen fidem in se, & ex sua natura, sive adjunctam habeat charitatem, sive non, esse primam & maxime necessariam dispositionem ad justitiam consequendam. Quoniam, scilicet, fides in se spectata est primus animae actus quo Deo conjungimur. Adeoque per fidem quae nondum formata est impetratur charitas qua postea formetur, si tamen id fiat quod fides suggerit, id est, si oratio fidei adhibeatur. Ut videre est apud eundem Stapletonum de Justificatione, lib. 8. qui est de Fide justificante, cap. 17.
pass_a_gloss: Although Rome admits dead and unformed faith does no good for salvation and is useless for justice, as Stapleton often says, they still teach that faith in itself, from its own nature, whether charity is joined or not, is the first and most necessary disposition for obtaining justice. Faith considered in itself is the first act of the soul by which we are joined to God. Through faith not yet formed, charity is obtained by which it is afterward formed, if what faith suggests is done, that is, if the prayer of faith is applied. See Stapleton, De Justificatione book 8, chapter 17.
pass_b_english: Even after granting with Stapleton that dead unformed faith profits neither salvation nor justice, Roman doctors still call faith as such, charity present or absent, the first and most necessary disposition toward justice.

In itself faith is the soul first act of union with God; by not-yet-formed faith charity is sought so that faith may later be formed, provided the prayer faith prompts is used (Stapleton, De Justif. 8.17).
